le-chatelier-s1.title: Disturbing a PCl₅ equilibrium
le-chatelier-s1.text: A sealed 1.00 L flask holds PCl5, PCl3 and Cl2 at equilibrium at constant temperature: PCl5(g) ⇌ PCl3(g) + Cl2(g), Kc = 0.040. At 50 s, one change is made to the flask. The graph shows the three concentrations.

le-chatelier-s2.title: The pink and blue cobalt equilibrium
le-chatelier-s2.text:
In water, cobalt(II) ions take part in this equilibrium:

Co(H2O)62+(aq) + 4 Cl−(aq) ⇌ CoCl42−(aq) + 6 H2O(l)
pink                       blue

A student starts with a purple solution (both ions present) in five test tubes and makes one change to each.

table.caption: Observations
rows: a few drops of concentrated HCl(aq), a source of Cl<sup>−</sup>, added
AgNO<sub>3</sub>(aq) added; a white solid forms

items.q: What change was made at 50 s?
options: Cl<sub>2</sub> was added.
PCl<sub>5</sub> was added.
The temperature was raised.
The volume was halved.

why.correct: A sudden vertical jump in one curve means that substance was added (or removed, for a drop). Gradual changes afterward are the system’s response.
options: Right: [Cl₂] jumps straight up at 50 s while the other two do not jump.
Added PCl₅ would make the PCl₅ curve jump. It rises gradually, as a result of the shift.
A temperature change does not make one concentration jump; the curves would bend smoothly to new values.
Halving the volume would make all three concentrations jump at once.

items.q: Which statement describes the response after 50 s?
options: The net reaction runs in reverse, using some of the added Cl<sub>2</sub>.
The net reaction runs forward, making more Cl<sub>2</sub>.
There is no net reaction, because K has not changed.
The net reaction runs in reverse until [Cl<sub>2</sub>] is back to its old value.

why.correct: Adding a product makes the system shift toward reactants, partly using up what was added. It does not undo the change completely.
options: Right: [Cl₂] and [PCl₃] fall while [PCl₅] rises, the reverse direction, which partly uses up the added Cl₂.
More Cl₂ forming would push [Cl₂] even higher. It falls after the jump.
K is unchanged, but Q has changed, so the system must react until Q = K again.
The shift only partly counteracts the change: [Cl₂] ends above its old value.

items.q: At the new equilibrium, [PCl<sub>3</sub>] = 0.039 M. Calculate the new [PCl<sub>5</sub>].

mistakes.why: Value: the reverse reaction makes PCl₅, so [PCl₅] goes up by the same amount [PCl₃] goes down.
Value: [PCl₅] changes during the shift. Add the amount of PCl₃ that reacted.

why.correct: Before the change: [PCl₃] = 0.072 M, [PCl₅] = 0.128 M. PCl₃ fell by 0.033 M, and the coefficients are 1 : 1, so PCl₅ rose by the same: 0.128 + 0.033 = 0.161 M.

items.q: How does K<sub>c</sub> after 100 s compare with K<sub>c</sub> before 50 s?
options: It is the same, 0.040.
It is larger, because more Cl<sub>2</sub> is present.
It is smaller, because the reaction shifted in reverse.
It is undefined until the added Cl<sub>2</sub> is used up.

why.correct: K depends only on temperature. A concentration change shifts the equilibrium position, not the constant.
options: Right: the temperature did not change, so K did not change. The concentrations rearranged to fit the same K.
Adding Cl₂ changed Q, not K. The system shifted until Q equaled the original K.
A shift changes concentrations, not K.
The added Cl₂ is never all used up, and K is defined at any equilibrium.

items.q: Compare the new equilibrium (after 100 s) with the original equilibrium (before 50 s).

variables.name: [PCl<sub>5</sub>]
variables.why: The reverse shift made more PCl₅.

variables.name: [PCl<sub>3</sub>]
variables.why: The reverse shift used some PCl₃.

variables.name: [Cl<sub>2</sub>]
variables.why: The shift used only part of the added Cl₂, so it ends higher than before.

why.correct: Adding a product shifts the equilibrium toward reactants. The added species ends higher than before, the other product lower, the reactant higher; K is unchanged.

items.q: What do tubes 2 and 3 show about the forward reaction?
options: It is endothermic.
It is exothermic.
It is faster when cold.
It does not depend on temperature.

why.correct: For an endothermic reaction, heat acts like a reactant: adding heat shifts the equilibrium forward (blue), removing heat shifts it back (pink).
options: Right: heating shifts the equilibrium toward the blue product, so the forward reaction absorbs heat.
If it were exothermic, heating would shift toward the reactants and turn the tube pink. It turned blue.
The colors show where equilibrium lies, not how fast it is reached.
The color changed with temperature, so the equilibrium position did.
Ag<sup>+</sup> removes Cl<sup>−</sup> as AgCl(s).
Ag<sup>+</sup> adds to the blue ion, turning it pink.
Adding a solution dilutes the tube, which turns it pink.
NO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> reacts with the pink ion.

why.correct: Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s) removes a reactant. The equilibrium shifts toward the side that makes Cl⁻: the pink side.
options: Right: lowering [Cl⁻], a reactant, makes the system shift in reverse to replace some of it.
The white solid is AgCl. The color change comes from the shift, not from silver joining a cobalt ion.
A few drops of solution barely dilute it. The precipitate shows Cl⁻ is being removed.
Nitrate is a spectator ion here; Ag⁺ is the active ion.

items.q: How does K<sub>c</sub> in tube 2 compare with K<sub>c</sub> in tube 1?
options: Greater: higher T, endothermic forward reaction.
The same, because no substance was added.
Smaller, because the reaction shifted toward the products.
The same, because K is a constant.

why.correct: Temperature is the one change that alters K. For an endothermic forward reaction, a higher temperature means a larger K.
options: Right: raising the temperature of an endothermic reaction increases K, which is why the mixture shifts toward the blue product.
K stays the same for concentration changes, but a temperature change alters K itself.
A shift toward products at higher temperature means K got larger, not smaller.
K is constant only at a fixed temperature.

items.q: In tube 4, why does the solution turn blue?
options: Added Cl<sup>−</sup> shifts the equilibrium forward.
HCl raises the temperature of the solution.
Added Cl<sup>−</sup> increases K.
HCl removes water, the product.

why.correct: Adding a reactant shifts the equilibrium toward the products, partly using up what was added.
options: Right: the system uses some of the added Cl⁻, making more blue CoCl₄²⁻.
A few drops at room temperature have little heating effect; tube 4 is not in a bath.
Adding a reactant changes Q, not K.
The drops add a little water, if anything. The key change is the added Cl⁻.

items.q: For N<sub>2</sub>(g) + 3 H<sub>2</sub>(g) ⇌ 2 NH<sub>3</sub>(g), ΔH° = −92 kJ/mol<sub>rxn</sub>, at equilibrium in a sealed container. Predict how the amount of NH<sub>3</sub> at the new equilibrium compares with before each change.

variables.name: The volume of the container is halved
variables.why: Smaller volume favors the side with fewer gas molecules: 2 NH₃ versus 4 reactant molecules.

variables.name: The temperature is raised
variables.why: The forward reaction is exothermic, so heat acts as a product; adding heat shifts the equilibrium in reverse.

variables.name: A catalyst is added
variables.why: A catalyst speeds both directions equally; the equilibrium amounts do not change.

variables.name: Some H<sub>2</sub> is removed
variables.why: Removing a reactant shifts the equilibrium in reverse to replace some of it.

why.correct: Le Châtelier’s principle: a change in concentration, volume or temperature makes the equilibrium shift to partly counteract it. A catalyst causes no shift.

items.q: For H<sub>2</sub>(g) + I<sub>2</sub>(g) ⇌ 2 HI(g) at equilibrium in a sealed container fitted with a movable piston, predict the effect on the amount of HI.

variables.name: The volume is doubled at constant temperature
variables.why: Both sides have 2 mol of gas, so a volume change affects reactants and products equally and causes no shift.

variables.name: Argon is added at constant volume
variables.why: An inert gas at constant volume changes no partial pressure or concentration of the reacting gases.

variables.name: More I<sub>2</sub> is added
variables.why: Adding a reactant shifts the equilibrium forward.

variables.name: Some HI is removed
variables.why: The shift replaces only part of the HI that was removed, so the amount of HI ends lower than before.

why.correct: Volume changes shift an equilibrium only when the gas moles differ on the two sides. Inert gases at constant volume and catalysts cause no shift.

items.q: For 2 SO<sub>2</sub>(g) + O<sub>2</sub>(g) ⇌ 2 SO<sub>3</sub>(g), ΔH° = −198 kJ/mol<sub>rxn</sub>, which change increases the value of K?
options: Cooling the mixture
Adding more O<sub>2</sub>
Decreasing the volume
Adding a catalyst

why.correct: Only temperature changes K. For an exothermic reaction (heat is a product), lowering the temperature increases K.
options: Right: for an exothermic reaction, cooling favors the products and increases K.
This shifts the equilibrium forward but does not change K.
This shifts toward fewer gas moles (products), but K stays the same.
A catalyst changes neither K nor the equilibrium position.

items.q: For N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>(g) ⇌ 2 NO<sub>2</sub>(g), the volume of an equilibrium mixture is suddenly halved at constant temperature. What happens to the brown color?
options: It darkens at once, then fades partway.
It fades at once, because the system shifts toward N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>.
It darkens and stays at that darker shade.
It does not change, because K does not change.

why.correct: Compression doubles every concentration first. Then the equilibrium shifts toward the side with fewer gas molecules, partly counteracting the change. [NO₂] ends higher than before the change but lower than right after it.
options: Right: halving the volume doubles [NO₂] instantly; the shift toward fewer gas molecules then lowers it partway.
The first effect is compression, which doubles [NO₂]. The shift comes after and only partly undoes it.
The system responds: it shifts toward N₂O₄ (fewer gas molecules), lowering [NO₂] somewhat.
K is unchanged, but the concentrations are not.

items.q: For C(s) + H<sub>2</sub>O(g) ⇌ CO(g) + H<sub>2</sub>(g), ΔH° = +131 kJ/mol<sub>rxn</sub>, which changes shift the equilibrium toward the products? Select all that apply.
options: Raising the temperature
Increasing the volume
Adding more C(s)
Adding a catalyst

why.correct: Count only gas moles for volume changes (the solid does not count), and treat heat as a reactant for an endothermic reaction.
options: Right: the forward reaction is endothermic, so heat acts as a reactant.
Right: products have 2 mol gas, reactants 1 mol gas, so more room favors the products.
A pure solid does not appear in Q, so adding it causes no shift.
A catalyst causes no shift.

items.q: A student explains: "Adding more N<sub>2</sub> to the ammonia equilibrium makes K bigger, so more NH<sub>3</sub> forms." What is wrong with this explanation?
options: K is unchanged; the added N<sub>2</sub> upsets the equilibrium.
Nothing is wrong; adding a reactant raises K.
Adding N<sub>2</sub> makes K smaller, so less NH<sub>3</sub> forms.
Adding N<sub>2</sub> has no effect, because N<sub>2</sub> is unreactive.

why.correct: K depends only on temperature. Adding a reactant disturbs the equilibrium (topic 7.10 shows how to state this with Q), and the system shifts forward.
options: Right: the shift happens because the mixture is out of balance with the same K, not because K changed.
Concentration changes never change K. Only temperature does.
K is unchanged, and adding a reactant shifts toward products.
N₂ is a reactant here; adding it does shift the equilibrium.
